title: What is the difference between @MappedSuperclass and @Inheritance in JPA? When do you use shared fields versus a real polymorphic type hierarchy?

s1_definition.profdef: `@MappedSuperclass` is a non-entity base class that holds **shared mapping information** (columns, audit fields) which subclasses inherit as their own columns; it is **not** an entity, has no table, and you **cannot** query it polymorphically or have associations point to it. `@Inheritance` sets up a **real entity type hierarchy** where the base class is itself an `@Entity`, the subclasses are entities, and JPA supports polymorphic queries (query the base type and get all subtypes) and polymorphic associations. Use `@MappedSuperclass` purely to share common columns and behaviour; use `@Inheritance` when the subtypes are genuinely different kinds of the same thing that you need to treat polymorphically.
s1_definition.analogy: `@MappedSuperclass` is like a standard header block (account number, created date, created by) that every account form reuses by copying it onto their own form — there is no separate "header" file and you cannot ask "show me all headers." `@Inheritance` is like saying "Account is a real category, and Savings Account and Current Account are specific kinds of Account" — you can walk into the records room and ask "give me all accounts" and receive both savings and current accounts together, because Account genuinely exists as a queryable type.
s1_definition.oneliner: @MappedSuperclass shares columns with subclasses but is not an entity (no polymorphic queries); @Inheritance makes a real entity hierarchy you can query and associate polymorphically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@MappedSuperclass` is a non-entity base class that holds **shared mapping information** (columns, audit fields) which subclasses inherit as their own columns; it is **not** an entity, has no table, and you **cannot** query it polymorphically or have associations point to it. `@Inheritance` sets up a **real entity type hierarchy** where the base class is itself an `@Entity`, the subclasses are entities, and JPA supports polymorphic queries (query the base type and get all subtypes) and polymorphic associations. Use `@MappedSuperclass` purely to share common columns and behaviour; use `@Inheritance` when the subtypes are genuinely different kinds of the same thing that you need to treat polymorphically.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `@MappedSuperclass` is like a standard header block (account number, created date, created by) that every account form reuses by copying it onto their own form — there is no separate "header" file and you cannot ask "show me all headers." `@Inheritance` is like saying "Account is a real category, and Savings Account and Current Account are specific kinds of Account" — you can walk into the records room and ask "give me all accounts" and receive both savings and current accounts together, because Account genuinely exists as a queryable type.

**One line to remember:** @MappedSuperclass shares columns with subclasses but is not an entity (no polymorphic queries); @Inheritance makes a real entity hierarchy you can query and associate polymorphically.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — the same audit columns were copy-pasted into every entity.** At National Bank of India, createdAt, createdBy, and a version column were duplicated across Account, LoanApplication, and Payment, and a change to the audit convention meant editing many classes. A `@MappedSuperclass` centralizes these shared columns. This is exactly the shared-fields use case.

**Problem 2 — a report must list "all accounts" regardless of whether they are savings or current.** The reporting module needs to query the Account type and get both subtypes, and a Transaction must reference "an Account" polymorphically. This needs a real entity hierarchy. This is exactly the `@Inheritance` use case.

What the code will do: an `Auditable` `@MappedSuperclass` with audit fields and a `@PrePersist` stamp, and a separate `@Inheritance` hierarchy where Account is an entity with SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount subtypes, demonstrating a polymorphic query.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: query all accounts; the table holds one SAVINGS and one CURRENT row.

Step 1 — the JPQL `select a from Account a` targets the base entity type. This is only valid because Account is a real entity with `@Inheritance`; if Account were a `@MappedSuperclass`, this query would be illegal.

Step 2 — Hibernate reads the accounts table and uses the account_type discriminator column to decide which subclass to instantiate for each row: SAVINGS rows become SavingsAccount, CURRENT rows become CurrentAccount.

Step 3 — the audit columns created_at and created_by, which came from the `Auditable` `@MappedSuperclass`, are populated on each instance just like any other inherited column.

Step 4 — the service iterates the list as `Account` and calls the polymorphic `kind()` method, which dispatches to the subtype's implementation, printing savings-specific and current-specific details.

Step 5 — on insert (not shown in this query), the inherited `@PrePersist` stamp from `Auditable` would set created_at and created_by automatically for any subtype, demonstrating shared behaviour from the mapped superclass.

```
2026-10-24 01:24:30 DEBUG Hibernate: select a.id, a.account_type, a.balance, a.interest_rate, a.overdraft_limit, a.created_at, a.created_by from accounts a
2026-10-24 01:24:30 INFO  SAV2001 balance=1000000.00 kind=SAVINGS @ 0.0400 created=2026-10-24T01:24:30
2026-10-24 01:24:30 INFO  CUR3001 balance=250000.00 kind=CURRENT od=50000.00 created=2026-10-24T01:24:30
```

```
  select a from Account a   (polymorphic — needs @Inheritance)
    │

    │  discriminator account_type
    ├─ 'SAVINGS' → instantiate SavingsAccount (interest_rate)
    └─ 'CURRENT' → instantiate CurrentAccount (overdraft_limit)

  ── @MappedSuperclass alone ──

```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — @MappedSuperclass vs @Inheritance (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Template Method: Account.kind() overridden per subtype     │
  │  Layer Supertype: Auditable shares audit mapping            │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  L: SavingsAccount/CurrentAccount usable wherever Account is │
  │  O: new account subtype = new @Entity subclass, no rewrites  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ Auditable @MappedSuperclass│  (NO table, NO polymorphic query)
  │ - createdAt, createdBy     │
  │ @PrePersist stamp()        │
  └───────────┬────────────────┘ extends
              ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────┐  @Entity @Inheritance(SINGLE_TABLE)
  │ Account (abstract @Entity) │  (REAL type — queryable, associable)
  │ - id, balance              │
  │ + kind(): String abstract  │
  └───────┬───────────┬────────┘
          ▼           ▼
  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
  │SavingsAccount│ │CurrentAccount│
  │ interestRate │ │ overdraftLim │
  │ kind()       │ │ kind()       │
  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘

  ── Decision (as prose) ──
  @MappedSuperclass: share columns/behaviour only; NOT an entity; no
     polymorphic query; no association target; each subclass has own table.
  @Inheritance: real entity hierarchy; polymorphic queries + associations;
     then pick SINGLE_TABLE / JOINED / TABLE_PER_CLASS.

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. select from Account (base)  2. discriminator → subtype
  3. audit cols from Auditable  4. iterate → kind() dispatch

  (Caution) cannot query/associate a @MappedSuperclass. (Caution) @Inheritance forces a strategy.
  Rule: shared columns → @MappedSuperclass; real polymorphic type → @Inheritance.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A mapped superclass is a non-entity base class that holds shared mapping information, like audit columns and an id strategy, which each entity subclass inherits as its own columns. The crucial point is that it is not an entity: there is no table for it, I cannot find it by id, I cannot write a query against it, and no relationship can point to it. Each subclass is completely independent at the database level and simply reuses the column definitions, so it is purely a code-reuse mechanism to avoid duplicating common mappings.

Inheritance, by contrast, creates a real entity type hierarchy. The base class is itself an entity carrying the inheritance annotation, and the subclasses are entities, which means the base type is queryable and associable polymorphically. I can write a query against the base type and get every subtype back in one result, and an association can reference the base type and hold any subtype. That is what I need when the subtypes are genuinely different kinds of the same thing that I sometimes treat uniformly and sometimes specifically, dispatching behavior by their real runtime type.

At National Bank of India I used both, and that is the clean answer. I had audit columns, created at, created by, and a version, copy-pasted across many entities, so I pulled them into a mapped superclass with a pre-persist callback that stamps them automatically, and every entity inherits those columns and that behavior. Separately, our reporting needed to list all accounts regardless of whether they were savings or current, and transactions needed to reference an account polymorphically, so Account is a real entity hierarchy with savings and current subtypes, and a single query against Account returns both. The nuances I always mention are that choosing inheritance forces a second decision about the strategy, whether single table, joined, or table per class, each with different table shapes and performance, that a mapped superclass can define inherited relationships and lifecycle callbacks and its columns can be overridden per subclass, and that the two mechanisms combine naturally, a mapped superclass for shared audit fields sitting above a real inheritance hierarchy for the actual types.

---

keyPoints: @MappedSuperclass: shared fields, NO polymorphic queries, no own table
@Inheritance: real type hierarchy, polymorphic queries, own table(s)
MappedSuperclass for: base audit fields (createdAt, updatedAt)
